title: Context Engineering in 2026 — Louis-François Bouchard, Omar Solano & Samridhi Vaid, Towards AI

primary.label: Context Engineering & Memory

domains.rationale: Best-fit classification from the supplied transcript and taxonomy.

summary: Bouchard completes context engineering: progressive-disclosure memory (~450-token LLM-wiki index), prompt-caching economics (cached tokens up to 50× cheaper with DeepSeek, compaction must shrink context >50× to break even), and Opik logging. Solano details the tutor: a single LangChain ReAct agent with create_agent, in-memory saver, middleware (5k-clear tool outputs, 30k-summarize), FastAPI/Next.js wrapping, and two tools over an 8M-token corpus—hybrid retrieve_tutor_context (CoHERE + BM25, top-30 → reranked top-5, 100k cap) and run_knowledgebase_command. The browse tool (raw markdown, generated titles, Claude-Code-built wiki, read-only bash, 8s timeout, 40k char cap, 20 commands/turn) was invoked ~90% of turns but measured identical recall at ~50% higher latency, so dropped. An evaluation harness ran 11 presets on 60 real student Q&A pairs (Gemini 2.5 Flash, Codex LLM-as-judge). Vaid extends to DeepSeek V3/Flash: full history wins on cost (97% cache hits, cheapest preset sent the most tokens), recall (95% vs 32% after summarizing), and latency, surviving 800k tokens. At scale, DeepSeek is ~$18k-$180k/month; local MacBook caps at 32k. On long contexts, dense retrieval drops to 0% at 400k tokens while BM25 stays at 100%. Final choice: DeepSeek V3/Flash + hybrid retrieval + keep-everything up to 30k tokens.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: Summarization is a trap: rewriting context invalidates prompt caches, so compaction must shrink context by >50× to break even on DeepSeek's 50× cached-token discount.
Context engineering = deciding per call what the model sees; keep, drop, or compact, and when.
The cheapest preset sent the most tokens: 97% cache hit rate made full-history cheaper than any compaction on DeepSeek V3/Flash.
Memory recall: full history 95% vs 32% after summarizing; distinctive facts survived up to 800k tokens with no visible rot.
Hardware changes the answer: a 32k MacBook window forces compaction because lessons exceed it; larger parameter count does not buy a larger window.
Dense retrieval fell to 0% at 400k tokens while BM25 stayed at 100%—hybrid search is essential.
Production defaults are unproven: 5k-clear/30k-summarize scored worse than 'do nothing' on cost, latency, and recall.
Name your real constraint (cache pricing, local window) before reaching for compaction.
Cloud keeps everything scored 92-95%; the same setup locally was stuck at 33% due to the 32k window.
Final setup: DeepSeek V3/Flash + hybrid retrieval + keep-everything up to 30k tokens.

sections.title: Offloading to files, the LLM wiki, and RAG
sections.summary: After compaction, the next lever is offloading to files (reversible, no information loss, ready for re-reference) plus RAG. GraphRAG was tested and tied plain RAG on real-user evaluations while being 'way costlier to set up,' so they skipped it. Truncated mid-thought about LLM wiki chunking.

sections.title: The LLM wiki, progressive disclosure, and small composable skills
sections.summary: RAG is cheap, durable, and inspectable. The tutor's LLM wiki stores everything as small chunks cross-linked by pointers to raw data files, exposed to the agent as a single ~450-token index. The agent scans the index, drills into chunks, and may descend to raw data—pulling more context for complex tasks and less for simple ones. Industry is converging on small, precise skills that reference each other and spawn sub-agents.

sections.title: Prompt caching and why compaction can backfire
sections.summary: Follow-up questions force recomputation of all previous tokens, so providers offer prompt caching with KV/embedding reuse—up to 50× cheaper with DeepSeek. Any compaction creates a new context that cannot match the cached prefix, so the rewrite must shrink context by >50× to pay off. Caching also speeds time-to-first-token because cached tokens are pre-computed.

sections.title: When to clear, compact, and optimize for cache hits
sections.summary: Bouchard's guidance: clear sessions on topic changes, use progressive disclosure for skills/files, clear stale tool outputs, compact selectively, and explicitly optimize for cache hits. Serious harnesses (Claude Code, Codex) do this. Logging everything via Opik/OpenTelemetry (cache hit rate, user frustration, abnormal outputs) is essential. Context engineering is defined as deciding per call what the model sees.

sections.title: The tutor's architecture: a single ReAct agent
sections.summary: The AI tutor is a single ReAct agent built with LangChain's create_agent and an in-memory saver (no cross-session memory), customized via middleware (summarize, clear tool outputs, source selection), wrapped in FastAPI with a Next.js UI, exposing two tools: retrieve_tutor_context (hybrid search) and run_knowledgebase_command (Karpathy-style wiki browsing).

sections.title: Hybrid search over an 8 million token corpus
sections.summary: The tutor's corpus contains all Towards AI course lessons plus docs for langchain, llama-index, OpenAI/Codex, and Claude Code—over 8M tokens, too large for a single window. Users pre-filter by source. Retrieval is hybrid: CoHERE embeddings + BM25 over a keyword index return top-30 chunks, merged and reranked to top-5, then hard-capped at 100k tokens by trimming the tail. Top-k and cap chosen empirically to maximize 'did we retrieve the correct page' recall.

sections.title: Letting the agent browse the knowledge base
sections.summary: Hybrid retrieval is precise, but some questions need the agent to traverse the corpus (e.g., comparing Codex and Claude Code). A cited paper motivates a second tool, run_knowledgebase_command, that lets the agent browse the knowledge base like a coding agent reads a codebase. Results on that tool follow.

sections.title: Browse tool filesystem: raw, generated titles, wiki
sections.summary: The browse tool exposes three folders: 'raw' with all markdown lessons and library docs; an auto-generated folder of titles for easy lookup; and a 'wiki' folder Claude Code built by reading raw files into a concise set of topic/framework files (e.g., a finetuning topic linking to all relevant raw files). In production the agent is restricted to read-only bash commands, with an 8-second timeout, 40,000-character output cap (forcing chained reads of long lessons), and a 20-command/turn cap; it is sandboxed to only browse the knowledge-base folder.

sections.title: Browse tool measured: same recall, 50% slower
sections.summary: The wiki is rebuilt only when new courses are added. The browse tool is invoked on ~90% of production turns (not optimized for). Most importantly, it was measured on real student questions: recall was identical to hybrid search alone, and latency was ~50% higher because of extra tool calls. The team concluded the second tool added no benefit and dropped it from the live tutor.

sections.title: The tutor's initial context engineering defaults
sections.summary: The tutor's original 'production' defaults were three middleware rules: clear tool outputs after 5,000 tokens (keep the last 5), summarize after 30,000 tokens (keep the last 20 messages for accuracy), and let the user select sources. These were unproven—chosen because 'it looks good'—motivating the empirical evaluation that follows.

sections.title: Live tutor demo on Hugging Face
sections.summary: Live demo of the tutor on Hugging Face: a separate UI for selecting sources, sending queries, and inspecting activity logs. Gemini 2.5 Flash reasoned, called tools, and produced a final answer citing 10 sources after four thought steps. Every turn is logged with input/output tokens, cached tokens, cost, time-to-first-token, tool-call count, and any summarization events—these logs drive the upcoming measurements.

sections.title: Defining experiment vocabulary
sections.summary: Four terms: a 'preset' is a specific AI tutor configuration (e.g., summarize at N tokens, sliding window); a 'task' is a single-turn or multi-turn session; a 'run' is one preset on one task; a 'bundle' is the resulting JSON with all metrics.

sections.title: Single-turn task: 60 real student Q&A pairs
sections.summary: Single-turn questions were not synthetic: Codex scraped Q&A from the Towards AI website where students ask staff, yielding a real dataset. Cleaning removed outdated library-version questions and duplicates, leaving 60 pairs. Grading is automated on (1) did retrieval return the correct lesson and (2) does the answer contain the correct facts/response—done by code checks and an LLM-as-judge, run cheaply via a Codex subscription rather than API.

sections.title: Multi-turn session task: facts, filler, probe
sections.summary: Multi-turn sessions test memory recall: a fake student states a fact (e.g., 'I want to learn about RAG evaluation'), filler messages pad the conversation, and a probe query asks the tutor to recall that fact (e.g., 'what should I learn today?' expecting 'RAG evaluation, specifically hit rate and MRR'). A gate check confirms that summarization actually fired in summarization presets before saving the run.

sections.title: Evaluation harness and grading
sections.summary: The harness's run_task_battery function runs each preset on each task. Grading combines code checks (correct lesson retrieved?) with an LLM-as-judge (correct facts?) using a Codex subscription. A check_triggers function confirms compaction actually fired before the run is saved. A generated report covers latency, time-to-first-token, and every logged metric, so runs can be evaluated and graded offline.

sections.title: Eleven presets across single-turn and session tasks
sections.summary: Eleven presets were run on each task while keeping the model, prompt, tools, and dataset fixed: 'full history' (do nothing), production defaults (5k-clear, 30k-summarize), and six techniques (sliding window, prompt compression, selective retention, etc.). Running all 11 cost over $500, motivating cheaper experiments.

sections.title: Results: doing nothing wins on all three fronts
sections.summary: Initial 11-preset results on Gemini 2.5 Flash with 11-13-turn sessions: not touching the context was the best strategy for memory recall; production defaults were not the best. The full-history preset is cheaper, faster, and has better recall overall. Latency is lower because removing tool outputs forces the agent to re-retrieve information it already had, increasing tool calls, token use, and cost. Single-turn tasks showed high recall across techniques because there were not enough tokens to trigger compaction. Multi-turn recall degraded to 38% with compaction versus full history. Initial runs used one or two trials, so rankings are indicative.

sections.title: Should you ever compact? Three new contexts
sections.summary: Samridhi introduces her section, noting the initial eval cost ~$600 and asking when compaction actually matters. Three context scenarios need separate evaluation: (1) cached chats with long chat history where details get buried, (2) pasted documents common in the tutor, and (3) internal tool logs that accumulate. Each context needs its own fix, so the extended evaluation covers all three.

sections.title: DeepSeek V3/Flash: same result, much cheaper
sections.summary: First extended test used DeepSeek V3/Flash as a cheaper model. Cost difference vs Gemini is drastic because DeepSeek's cache discount is 50×. Even on DeepSeek, keeping the full history wins. On specific-detail queries the model recalled 95% with full history versus 32% after summarizing—summarization removes the necessary details.

sections.title: Cost at scale and long-context recall
sections.summary: On DeepSeek, the setup sending the most tokens was the cheapest: 97% of tokens were cached and cached tokens are charged separately. Summarization forces the model to read and write new tokens every turn. A 36-turn conversation at ~1.78M tokens still favored full history. Distinctive facts were recovered consistently up to 800k tokens with no visible rot; ambiguous-fact recall dropped to roughly half. The model holds up well on long conversations without compaction.

sections.title: Going local and hardware-limited context windows
sections.summary: Per-turn cost is only one axis; chatbot scale (100k-1M turns/day) drives real spend. DeepSeek at that volume is ~$18k-$180k/month. The alternative is local models that also cache. Tested on a MacBook capped at a 32k window: lessons already exceed 32k, so caching no longer helps and compaction or retrieval becomes mandatory. Keeping everything stops winning locally because it cannot fit. A larger parameter count does not buy a larger window—GPUs and MacBooks both have hardware limits.

sections.title: Local limits, parameter count, and retrieval vs stuffing
sections.summary: Increasing model size from 7B/8B to 32B did not increase the local context window. For pasted documents locally, RAG gave 100% accuracy in 25-65 seconds. Stuffing the window with more context than it can hold was wasteful—long conversations took ~340s to produce a single output token. Retrieval is preferable to stuffing. Dense RAG worked at ~80% from 50k-200k tokens but dropped to 0% recall at 400k on facts buried in the middle, while BM25 still got 100%—semantic search alone is not enough, which is why the tutor uses hybrid search.

sections.title: Cloud vs local side-by-side and full summary
sections.summary: Cloud-vs-local comparison: for chat, local was not up to par with cloud—keeping everything on cloud scored 92-95%, but locally it was stuck at 33% due to the 32k window. Local models work because there is no per-token cost (you own the hardware) but throughput is limited; retrieval gives good accuracy locally. Full results: 95% memory recall with full history vs 32% after summarizing; long-context single-fact recall is easy up to 800k tokens with no rot; cheapest run sent the most tokens due to caching; at scale Gemini cost ~$40,000/month vs DeepSeek ~$1,900/month for 1,000 students. The takeaway: do not compact by default; name the constraint and pick a better alternative.

sections.title: Final decision: DeepSeek V3/Flash + hybrid + keep-everything
sections.summary: Final choice: DeepSeek V3/Flash because hardware limitations made the cloud structure work best and it is the cheapest given current student intake. On top of that, they use hybrid retrieval for good results. For memory they chose to keep everything, with a 30k-token default limit after which compaction fires—everything below that is preserved. The full setup is in the fullstack AI engineering course on academy.towardsai.net.

organization.name: Towards AI
organization.summary: Towards AI, Inc. is an independent AI education and deployment company. First-party pages describe the world's leading AI practitioner community and Towards AI Academy, whose Full Stack AI Engineer course walks students through building the same AI tutor presented on stage. The official GitHub org publishes towardsai/ai-tutor-app, built by Louis-François Bouchard (CTO), Omar Solano, and Samridhi Vaid. DeepSeek and LangChain are models and libraries used in the experiments, not the implementation owner.
organization.status: Independent company as of the research date. towardsai.com, towardsai.net/community, the Academy, and github.com/towardsai/ai-tutor-app are live. No ownership change since the August 2026 talk.
